stem: A 67-year-old man with a long history of heavy smoking comes to the office due to blurry and distorted vision in his right eye.  His vision has declined over the past year and worsened over the past several weeks, making driving and reading difficult.  Funduscopic examination of the right eye reveals grayish discoloration of the macula with adjacent subretinal fluid and hemorrhage.  Which of the following mechanisms most likely contributed to this patient's condition?​‌​‌‌‌‌​​​‌‌‌‌‌​​‌‌‌‌‌​​​‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌​‌​‌​‌‌​‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​​‌‌​​​‌‌‌​‌​​​​‌​‌‌​‌​​‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌​​‌​​‌​​​​​​​‌‌‌​​​‌​‌‌‌​‌​‌​​‌​​‌​‌​‌‌​‌​‌‌‌​‌​‌​​​​​​‌​​‌‌‌​‌​‌‌​‌​‌​​​‌‌​​​​‌​‌‌‌‌‌​​‌​​‌‌​‌​‌‌​​‌​‌‌‌‌​‌‌​​​‌‌​​​​​‌​‌‌​‌​​​​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌​​​​‌‌​​​​​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌​‌‌​‌​‌​​​​‌​‌‌​‌‌‌​​​‌​‌​‌​‌‌​‌​​‌​​‌‌​​​‌​​‌‌​​​‌‌​‌‌‌‌​​‌‌​​‌​‌​​‌‌‌​​​​​​​​‌‌‌‌
explanation:
This patient likely has age-related macular degeneration (AMD), which is associated with advancing age and environmental factors (eg, smoking); it is classified into dry and wet subtypes.

Dry AMD is characterized by gradual central vision loss in one or both eyes and can cause difficulty with driving, reading, and recognizing faces.  The condition involves chronic oxidative damage (exacerbated by smoking) and inflammation affecting the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) and underlying tissues.  This leads to extracellular lipid and protein accumulation beneath the RPE (drusen) and eventual photoreceptor loss.

These changes can impair oxygen delivery to the outer retina and promote local vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) production.  VEGF stimulates choroidal neovascularization, in which abnormal vessels grow through Bruch membrane beneath the RPE or into the subretinal space.  This condition is termed wet AMD, as the fragile vessels tend to leak fluid or bleed, causing rapid vision loss (days to weeks) and metamorphopsia (distortion of straight lines).  Funduscopy may show a grayish-green subretinal membrane with adjacent fluid or hemorrhage.

All patients with AMD who smoke should receive smoking cessation counseling.  Wet AMD is treated with intravitreal VEGF inhibitors (eg, ranibizumab, bevacizumab), which reduce neovascularization and vascular leakage and can stabilize or improve vision.

(Choice A)  Chronic hyperglycemia causes retinal microvascular injury in diabetic retinopathy.  Funduscopic findings include microaneurysms, dot-blot hemorrhages, and cotton-wool spots; retinal ischemia can lead to neovascularization in proliferative disease.  These abnormalities typically extend beyond the macula.

(Choice B)  Retinitis pigmentosa is a group of inherited disorders characterized by progressive photoreceptor degeneration.  Patients typically develop night blindness followed by loss of peripheral vision, often beginning in childhood or adolescence.  Funduscopy reveals bone-spicule pigmentation, retinal vessel attenuation, and optic disc pallor.

(Choice C)  Increased intracranial pressure is transmitted through the subarachnoid space surrounding the optic nerve, disrupting axoplasmic flow at the optic nerve head and causing papilledema.  Findings include an enlarged blind spot and usually bilateral optic disc swelling.

(Choice D)  Elevated intraocular pressure can damage retinal ganglion cells and their axons (ie, glaucoma), causing optic nerve atrophy with progressive peripheral visual field loss and an increased cup/disc ratio.

Educational objective:Wet age-related macular degeneration is characterized by VEGF-mediated choroidal neovascularization.  Leakage or bleeding from these abnormal vessels causes rapid central vision loss and metamorphopsia, with funduscopy showing a grayish-green subretinal membrane and/or subretinal fluid or hemorrhage.​‌​‌‌‌‌​​​‌‌‌‌‌​​‌‌‌‌‌​​​‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌​‌​‌​‌‌​‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​​‌‌​​​‌‌‌​‌​​​​‌​‌‌​‌​​‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌​​‌​​‌​​​​​​​‌‌‌​​​‌​‌‌‌​‌​‌​​‌​​‌​‌​‌‌​‌​‌‌‌​‌​‌​​​​​​‌​​‌‌‌​‌​‌‌​‌​‌​​​‌‌​​​​‌​‌‌‌‌‌​​‌​​‌‌​‌​‌‌​​‌​‌‌‌‌​‌‌​​​‌‌​​​​​‌​‌‌​‌​​​​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌​​​​‌‌​​​​​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌​‌‌​‌​‌​​​​‌​‌‌​‌‌‌​​​‌​‌​‌​‌‌​‌​​‌​​‌‌​​​‌​​‌‌​​​‌‌​‌‌‌‌​​‌‌​​‌​‌​​‌‌‌​​​​​​​​‌‌‌‌
